title: Money on the Table: Why Better Budget Planning Is Key to Fixing the Water Crisis
gist: World Bank water and governance leaders argue the global water crisis is as much an execution problem as a financing problem: water-sector budget execution averaged only 72% globally (62% in Sub-Saharan Africa) from 2009-2020, and fixing it requires strengthening Public Financial Management and Public Investment Management systems rather than just raising more money — the thesis behind the Bank's new 'Water Forward' initiative.

themes.theme: The Spending Gap Within the Financing Gap

insights.claim: The World Bank Group's 2024 report 'Funding a Water-Secure Future' finds that global water-sector budget execution averaged only 72% between 2009 and 2020 — meaning roughly 28 cents of every allocated dollar for water is never actually spent.
insights.speaker: Saroj Kumar Jha, Arturo Herrera Gutierrez, Kaushiki Singh
insights.so_what: A quantified execution gap (28 cents on the dollar) means water-sector financing headlines overstate real infrastructure delivery — relevant for evaluating World Bank/donor water-project completion risk.
insights.quote: water sector budget execution averaged only 72 percent between 2009 and 2020
insights.locator: The Paradox: A Spending Gap Within a Financing Gap

insights.claim: Sub-Saharan Africa's water-sector budget execution rate averages only around 62%, notably worse than the 72% global average, even though the region has among the largest unmet water-access needs.
insights.speaker: Saroj Kumar Jha, Arturo Herrera Gutierrez, Kaushiki Singh
insights.so_what: Identifies Sub-Saharan Africa as the region where the execution gap is most acute relative to need — a priority zone for World Bank PFM/PIM technical-assistance lending.

insights.claim: The authors' central thesis is that countries are simultaneously failing to close the water financing gap and leaving allocated money unspent, implying that mobilizing more financing alone will not fix the water crisis without institutional execution reform.
insights.speaker: Saroj Kumar Jha, Arturo Herrera Gutierrez, Kaushiki Singh
insights.so_what: Reframes the water-crisis narrative from 'needs more capital' to 'needs better execution systems' — implies capital alone (e.g., new water bonds or blended finance) will underdeliver without paired PFM/PIM reform.
insights.locator: countries are failing to close the financing gap while also leaving allocated money on the table

insights.claim: The world is 'massively off-track' on Sustainable Development Goal 6 (clean water and sanitation for all by 2030), and the water sector is estimated to support 1.7 billion jobs worldwide.
insights.speaker: Saroj Kumar Jha, Arturo Herrera Gutierrez, Kaushiki Singh
insights.so_what: Establishes the macro stakes — 1.7bn jobs tied to a sector missing its 2030 UN target — for why execution reform (not just financing) matters at a global scale.
insights.quote: the world is massively off-track on Sustainable Development Goal 6

themes.theme: Why the Money Doesn't Get Spent

insights.claim: Water infrastructure projects stall not from lack of government will but from institutional bottlenecks: rushed project preparation, procurement requiring uncoordinated sign-offs from multiple agencies, and land acquisition/environmental clearance delays that consume most of the fiscal year before construction can begin — after which unspent funds return to the treasury.
insights.speaker: Saroj Kumar Jha, Arturo Herrera Gutierrez, Kaushiki Singh
insights.so_what: Names the specific mechanism (procurement coordination failure, land/environmental clearance timing) causing water-fund underspend — a template for diagnosing similar infrastructure-execution risk in other capital-intensive public sectors.
insights.locator: Why Does the Money Stay on the Table?

insights.claim: The authors frame a budget allocation as 'not a plan but a promise' — without a well-sequenced, multi-year program spanning land, design, procurement and construction, allocated water money will keep sitting unspent.
insights.speaker: Saroj Kumar Jha, Arturo Herrera Gutierrez, Kaushiki Singh
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for evaluating any government capital-spending announcement: allocation without a sequenced multi-year implementation plan is not credible delivery.
insights.quote: A budget allocation is not a plan but a promise.

themes.theme: PFM/PIM as the Fix, and the Water Forward Initiative

insights.claim: The authors distinguish Public Financial Management (PFM — how governments plan, allocate and spend money) from Public Investment Management (PIM — how they select, prepare and implement investment projects), arguing that weaknesses in either — no medium-term expenditure plan, no project pipeline, no alignment between sector goals and annual budgets — cause even well-funded water ministries to fail at converting allocations into infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Saroj Kumar Jha, Arturo Herrera Gutierrez, Kaushiki Singh
insights.so_what: A reusable diagnostic framework (PFM vs PIM) for assessing execution risk in any public infrastructure sector, not just water.
insights.locator: Where PFM and PIM Come In — and Why Water Forward Depends on Them

insights.claim: Using the PEFA (Public Expenditure and Financial Accountability) framework across a 22-country sample, 'budget reliability' (Pillar I) and 'policy-based fiscal strategy and budgeting' (Pillar IV) are the two dimensions most strongly associated with water-sector budget execution, with Pillar IV showing the stronger relationship.
insights.speaker: Saroj Kumar Jha, Arturo Herrera Gutierrez, Kaushiki Singh
insights.so_what: Identifies which specific PEFA reform lever (fiscal-strategy alignment over raw budget reliability) has the largest measured effect on execution — a prioritization signal for governance-reform lending.
insights.locator: Using the Public Expenditure and Financial Accountability (PEFA) framework, budget reliability along with policy-based fiscal strategy and budgeting emerge as the two dimensions most strongly associated with water-sector budget execution

insights.claim: The World Bank Group's 'Water Forward' initiative, through country-led 'Water Compacts,' aims to bundle policy reform, institutional strengthening, investment planning and financing into a single framework with governments, development partners and investors, explicitly trying to shift the conversation 'from financing to delivery.'
insights.speaker: Saroj Kumar Jha, Arturo Herrera Gutierrez, Kaushiki Singh
insights.so_what: Names the specific new World Bank vehicle (Water Forward / Water Compacts) to track for future water-sector blended-finance and governance-reform deals.
insights.quote: shift the conversation from financing to delivery
insights.locator: This is also where Water Forward can help
